subsection: 2. The historical development of the Irish family

notes.h: The Irish family before the 1960s (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Until the 1960s the Irish family was largely rural, agricultural and organised around the farm as an economic unit.
points: The extended family was common, with grandparents, unmarried relatives and children living in one household or close by.
Agriculture provided most employment, so family members worked together on the farm and shared its income.
Families were large, and high child mortality meant many children did not reach adulthood.
Authority was patriarchal: the father controlled decisions and finances, and discipline was authoritarian.
Gender roles were segregated, with men working outside the home and women responsible for housework and the children.
The Catholic Church had a strong influence on marriage, morality and family life.
Marriages were often arranged, and many people never married, particularly in rural areas.
Rural electrification in the 1940s eased the workload of mothers by bringing electric appliances and lighting to farm homes.

notes.h: The Irish family from the 1960s to the 1990s (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Industrial and economic change weakened the rural extended family and moved the family towards the nuclear form.
points: Free second-level education was introduced in 1967, so more children stayed in school for longer.
Industrialisation and the growth of services drew people from farms to towns and cities, loosening links with the extended family.
Couples married younger and increasingly married for love rather than for land or money.
Women's paid employment grew, and both parents could work outside the home, reducing the domestic role of women.
Wages rose and living standards improved, so families could afford more goods and better housing.
Contraception was legalised for married couples in 1979, and family size fell as couples chose to have fewer children.
Emigration stayed high during the 1980s, and many families were separated when adult children left to find work.

notes.h: Changes in family law (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Changes in the law made separation, divorce and other partnerships legally recognised, which altered family structure.
points: The Judicial Separation and Family Law Reform Act 1989 provided for judicial separation, allowing spouses to live apart under a court order on property and maintenance.
Divorce was approved by referendum in 1995, by a narrow majority.
The Family Law (Divorce) Act 1996 set out the conditions for divorce, including a period of living apart, and was later amended by the Family Law Act 2019.
Civil partnership, introduced in 2010, gave same-sex couples legal recognition and rights similar to those of marriage.
Same-sex marriage was approved by referendum in 2015, extending marriage to same-sex couples.

notes.h: The Irish family from the 1990s to the present (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Economic growth, legal change and the recession after 2008 reshaped family roles, living arrangements and family life abroad.
points: Dual-income families became common, and parents shared decisions and household tasks more equally.
Lone-parent and blended families grew as separation and divorce became legal options.
Demand for childcare rose as both parents worked, and families relied on creches, childminders and grandparents.
Role overload arose when parents cared for their own children and elderly parents at the same time.
The recession after 2008 brought unemployment, mortgage arrears and emigration, and some fathers became the main carers at home.
Family members often live abroad, and mobile phones, email and video calls keep relatives in contact across distances.

keyTerms.definition: A family including parents, children and wider relatives such as grandparents, aunts, uncles and cousins, who live in one household or close by.
A family made up of parents and their dependent children living in a self-contained household.
Family control held by the father, who makes the main decisions and controls finances.
The extension of mains electricity to rural homes, which reduced the domestic workload of women.
A court order allowing spouses to live apart with legal orders on property and maintenance, without ending the marriage.
A legal relationship between two people, introduced in Ireland in 2010, giving rights similar to those of marriage.
A family in which both parents have paid employment.
The strain of carrying out too many roles at once, such as caring for children and elderly parents.

factCards.term: Three features of the Irish family before the 1960s
factCards.definition: Extended family living arrangements; large families; the family as an agricultural economic unit.

factCards.term: Year free second-level education was introduced in Ireland
factCards.definition: 1967, under Minister for Education Donogh O'Malley.

factCards.term: Year divorce was approved in an Irish referendum
factCards.definition: 1995, followed by the Family Law (Divorce) Act 1996.

factCards.term: Year same-sex marriage was approved in an Irish referendum
Three changes in Irish family life from the 1990s
factCards.definition: Dual-income families; lone-parent and blended families; same-sex partnerships.

factCards.term: Two effects of the recession after 2008 on families
factCards.definition: Unemployment and mortgage arrears; emigration that separated families.

questions.prompt: Outline two ways in which the Irish family has changed since the 1960s.
questions.model: Two changes, each with explanation. For example: the decline of the rural extended family and the move to nuclear families as people moved from farms to towns; or dual-income families, with both parents working outside the home and sharing household tasks.

questions.prompt: Discuss the historical development of the Irish family from the beginning of the twentieth century to the present day, referring to family structure, family roles and family law.
questions.model: Early twentieth century: extended family common; large families; high child mortality; agriculture as economic base; patriarchal authority; segregated gender roles; strong Church influence. 1960s to 1990s: free second-level education from 1967; move from farms to towns; nuclear families; younger marriage for love; more women in paid work; contraception legal for married couples from 1979; smaller families; emigration. Family law: judicial separation from 1989; divorce approved in 1995 and provided for by the Family Law (Divorce) Act 1996; civil partnership from 2010; same-sex marriage from a 2015 referendum. Present day: dual-income families; shared roles; lone-parent and blended families; demand for childcare; role overload; recession after 2008 with emigration and stay-at-home fathers; communication technology keeping families in touch across distance.
